entry.title: Learning to Play
entry.content:
This month I have been reading The Infinity Machine, Sebastian Mallaby’s biography of Demis Hassabis, the chess prodigy from North London who founded DeepMind, the laboratory behind AlphaGo and AlphaFold. I picked it up because I wanted to understand one of the early architects of the AI we now live with, told by someone who had thirty hours of his time, and because almost everything that interests me, games, simulations, the question of what a machine can learn on its own, runs through his story. A hundred pages in, there is a scene I have not been able to put down.

It is 1988 and Hassabis is twelve. He has bought a Commodore Amiga 500 with his chess winnings, and in Foyles, the big bookshop on Charing Cross Road, he finds a slim paperback: The Chess Computer Handbook by David Levy. He reads it in one sitting. Levy explains how a chess program is built from three parts. The board has to be turned into numbers. A function has to look at a position and say who is better. And a search has to try moves, and the replies to them, and the replies to those, cutting off the branches that are obviously bad because the tree grows faster than any computer can follow. Hassabis tries to build it, finds that the Amiga chokes on chess, and writes an Othello program instead, which beats his five-year-old brother.

I put the book down at that point, partly because I recognised the boy a little, and partly because I realised two things. The first is that those three parts are still the whole of a chess program. Thirty-eight years later, the strongest engines in the world are a board in numbers, an evaluation function, and a tree search with pruning; what has changed is that the evaluation function is now learned by a machine rather than written by a person, and that the machine learned it by playing against itself. The second is that the laptop on my desk has thirty thousand times the memory of that Amiga, and I had never built the three parts myself.

So I did, this month. I wrote three game engines in Rust, for chess, for Japanese shogi, and for Go, compiled them to WebAssembly so they play in a browser on my phone, and built the training loop that is supposed to make one of them stronger than I could make it by hand. The app is at kishi.raskell.io and the code is on GitHub. This is an account of why those three games, why those tools, and what happened when the ideas in the books met one ordinary machine.

The book, the man and the lab

Mallaby is not a technology writer by trade. He is a former contributing editor of the Financial Times, twice a Pulitzer finalist, now a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, and his earlier books were about money: hedge funds in More Money Than God, Alan Greenspan in The Man Who Knew, venture capital in The Power Law. That turns out to be the right background. The Infinity Machine is a biography and a company history at once, built on about thirty hours of conversation with Hassabis and more than a hundred interviews around him, and it takes the question of why someone would build a technology they believe to be dangerous as seriously as the question of how. It came out earlier this year. I am reading it slowly, and the AlphaGo chapters are still ahead of me, which I find I do not mind, because I would rather meet them with my own version of the thing running.

Hassabis, if you do not follow the field, is the person it now treats as its elder statesman, at fifty. Born in Finchley in 1976 to a Singaporean Chinese mother and a Greek Cypriot father, he was a chess master at thirteen and the second-strongest player of his age in the world. At sixteen he was co-writing Theme Park at the games studio Bullfrog, a game that sold millions. He read computer science at Cambridge, ran a games studio of his own for seven years, and then went back to university for a doctorate in neuroscience, because he thought the only way to build an intelligent machine was to understand the one existing example first. In 2010, in an attic on Russell Square, he founded DeepMind with Shane Legg and Mustafa Suleyman, at a time when almost nobody in the field believed that what they proposed was possible. The first real money came from a Peter Thiel fund whose partners rated the science A-plus and the business model an F.

DeepMind was conceived as a Manhattan Project for artificial intelligence, and its method is what connects the book to this article. The bet was to combine two branches of the field that were both unfashionable in 2010: deep learning, the layered neural networks Geoffrey Hinton had spent a quarter of a century defending, and reinforcement learning, in which a program learns from the consequences of its own actions rather than from labelled examples, with ideas from neuroscience on top. The proving ground was games, because games have rules you can write down and scores you can read off the board. The first result, shown in 2013, was one agent that learned to play Atari games from the pixels alone. Google bought the company in 2014. In 2016 AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol in Seoul, and in 2017 its successor, AlphaZero, learned chess, shogi and Go from nothing but the rules and games against itself, with one algorithm, and beat the strongest existing program at each. Those are the three games in this article, in that order, and self-play is the loop I built. AlphaFold followed in 2020, then the predicted shapes of two hundred million proteins, then the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2024. Even the name is a triple nod: to deep learning, to Deep Blue, and to Deep Thought, the computer in The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy that was asked for the answer to everything.

Why am I reading it? Partly for the obvious reason: I work on AI platforms for a living and wanted the story of one of the architects of this revolution from the inside, and the book is exactly that and more. Partly because of the parallels, which kept catching me off guard: a games designer who smuggled a simulation into a theme park, a competitor who cannot pass a board game without wanting to win it, a man who thinks of the world as information and of the mind as something that builds reality rather than records it. I recognise more of that than is comfortable. And partly because of the belief. Hassabis believed in artificial intelligence when almost nobody did, with a conviction the book is honest enough to call close to religious, and he was right. There is a strand of transhumanism running through the story, from the Iain Banks novels he read at Bullfrog to the Singularity Summit where DeepMind found its first investor, and he keeps a dry British distance from the Californian version of it. I have a strand of my own, with a different spin and from a different direction, and that is a subject for another piece. It is enough to say here that I did not come to the book as a sceptic.

What hooked me in those early pages, more than the prodigy story, is how often games are the way in. Hassabis learns programming through chess. His first intelligent program plays Othello. At Cambridge he learns Go from a professor and takes shogi far enough to reach the top of the English rankings. His friend David Silver, who will later lead the AlphaGo work, finds his way into the field through a textbook on reinforcement learning, read in the south of France after their games company failed. Mallaby traces the thread back to Claude Shannon’s 1950 paper on programming a computer to play chess, which Levy’s handbook had introduced to the twelve-year-old. Shannon wrote that chess programs had no practical importance, but that mastering a game might serve as “a wedge in attacking other problems of a similar nature and of greater significance”. That sentence is seventy-six years old and still the best one-line justification I know for spending a month on board games.

My own games

My own chess is a smaller story. I joined a chess club in my early teens, played the regional tournaments, and did well in a few of them: nothing that would have sent a chess columnist across the hall to talk to my father, as one did for Hassabis when he was six, and nothing I would put in the same paragraph as his career if the book had not put the two of us in the same bookshop. But the game stayed. I do not turn down a game when one is offered; the last one was against a coworker and friend on Union Square in San Francisco, this year. I have a weakness for the big outdoor sets with knee-high pieces, and there are two I like, one in Lucerne and one beside the Rhine here in Basel. On trains I play on lichess on my phone. And I have enjoyed, more than I expected to, the odd second life the game found in the 2020s, when a television series about a fictional prodigy sent people out to buy boards and grandmasters turned into streamers with audiences no tournament hall could hold. I did not see that coming, and I am not complaining.

The other half of my gaming life is what German calls Aufbauspiele, the building games: Anno, Die Siedler, the whole tycoon genre, anything where you lay down a world with rules and watch it run. Hassabis’s Theme Park is one of them, which made that chapter feel personal. The visitors who get thirsty when you oversalt the fries and buy more drinks, the riders who are sick when the coaster is too fast, are exactly the kind of mechanism I play these games for. I like games best when they try to mimic reality and let a thick ruleset generate stories nobody wrote, which is why I love Dwarf Fortress, and it is why I keep building simulations of my own, from a dish of neurons that learns under stimulation to a terrarium left to evolve. A chess engine, seen from that side, is the smallest simulation worth building: a complete world with rules, and inside it an agent that has to learn.

Why games, and why these three

Shannon’s point is practical. A game like chess has rules you can write down completely, a result you can read off the board without argument, and a depth that no amount of study has exhausted. That combination is rare. Most real problems have fuzzy rules, contested outcomes and no yardstick. A game gives you a laboratory where a new idea can be tested in an afternoon, against centuries of human knowledge, and the answer is a number.

Chess, shogi and Go also happen to be the three games along which the history of this field unfolded, in that order, and each one broke what had worked on the one before. That is why I picked all three rather than one.

Chess came out of northern India around the sixth century as chaturanga, travelled through Persia into Europe, and took its modern form, with the long-range queen and bishop, in Spain and Italy at the end of the fifteenth century. It is the game Shannon chose, the game Levy’s handbook teaches, and the one the classical method of search plus evaluation was built for. In 1997 IBM’s Deep Blue beat Garry Kasparov by searching two hundred million positions a second on purpose-built chips, with an evaluation written and tuned by people. It was a triumph of the three parts and a disappointment to anyone hoping for insight: the machine won by looking further, not by understanding more. The interesting question, from Levy’s chapter onwards, was whether the evaluation function could be learned instead of written. For chess, that question was answered between 2018 and 2020 with a small neural network that lives inside the engine’s inner loop. It is called NNUE, and it was not invented for chess.

Shogi is the Japanese branch of the same family. It arrived in Japan by way of China and Southeast Asia by the eleventh century, took its present form by the sixteenth, and became an institution under the Tokugawa shoguns, who put the best players on stipends; the first Meijin, the title that still crowns a shogi champion, was awarded in 1612. Today it is played by millions in Japan, with a professional system, televised title matches, and a young star, Sota Fujii, who in 2023, at twenty-one, held all eight major titles at once. The board is nine by nine, each side has twenty pieces of eight kinds, and most of them promote when they reach the far third of the board. One rule makes it a different game. A captured piece changes sides, goes into the captor’s hand, and can later be dropped onto almost any empty square as a move. Nothing ever leaves the board for good, so the game never simplifies the way chess does. There are about eighty moves to choose from at a typical turn against chess’s thirty-five, the games are longer, and the endgame is a mutual race rather than a technical grind. For a programmer, drops make the evaluation function much harder to write by hand, which is why the learning happened here first. Computer shogi was transformed in 2006 by Bonanza, the first program whose evaluation was fitted to professional games rather than tuned by hand. In 2017 Ponanza beat the reigning Meijin, Amahiko Sato, and in 2018 Yu Nasu published the network design that Stockfish adopted for chess two years later. Shogi is where the idea I was chasing came from.

Go is older than both and simpler than either. It comes from China, where it is at least two and a half thousand years old and was counted among the four accomplishments of a cultivated person alongside music, calligraphy and painting; it reached Japan by the eighth century, where the Edo-period houses of professional players were funded by the shogunate, and it has deep roots in Korea, where it is called baduk. The rules fit on a card. Two players alternately place black and white stones on the intersections of a nineteen-by-nineteen grid. A group of stones with no empty points next to it is captured and removed. At the end, whoever surrounds more of the board wins, with a few points’ compensation to white for moving second. From those rules comes a game with around two hundred and fifty choices at every turn, games of two or three hundred moves, and positions that nobody has been able to score by hand. Levy’s three parts fail here. A search that looks four moves ahead in Go sees almost nothing, and there is no formula for who is winning to apply at the leaves. Go was the game that everyone in the field, including Hassabis, called the grand challenge, and it was the one DeepMind chose when it wanted to show what it had. The programs of the late 2000s had replaced the chess method with Monte Carlo tree search, which plays thousands of random games out to the end and counts who wins; that got to strong-amateur level and stuck. AlphaGo kept that search and gave it two neural networks, one to suggest moves and one to judge positions, trained first on human games and then on its own, and in March 2016 it beat Lee Sedol four games to one.

So: one game where the classical method works and the network replaces the evaluation; one where the same method strains and the network was invented; one where the method fails and the network has to guide the search itself. The three together are a short course in forty years of the field, and each one can be measured against opponents anyone can download.

Why I built it rather than read about it

Hassabis likes to cite Feynman’s line about not understanding what you cannot build, and it is the honest reason for this project. I have read the AlphaGo paper and the Stockfish NNUE write-ups more than once. I could explain the diagrams. I could not have told you what K is, or why a network that wins at equal search depth can lose at equal time, or how many hours of a laptop’s life a generation of self-play costs, because those are the things the papers leave out and the only way to learn them is to pay for them. Reading the book made the gap uncomfortable, and the same itch that makes me build terrariums wanted the world with the rules and the learner inside it running on my own machine.

The other reason is that the ingredients are, for the first time, all on my desk. The ideas are published and the reference implementations are open source. The laptop is a MacBook Pro with an Apple M4, ten cores and sixteen gigabytes of memory, which is not a research machine and has more general computing power than Deep Blue had. The browser on my phone can now run compiled code with vector instructions and real threads. And the writing of the code itself, which would have been a winter of evenings, took days with a coding agent, with me deciding what to build and the agent typing most of it. That belongs in the method: the agent wrote code, a match between two engines decided whether the code was any good, and the match does not care who wrote it.

Why Rust, and not PyTorch

The obvious way to do machine learning in 2026 is Python and PyTorch, and if the goal had been a model that answers questions on a server, that is what I would have used. The goal was an opponent on my phone, in a browser tab, offline, and that changed everything downstream.

A chess evaluation is called inside the search, about a million times a second, on one core, with no batching, rather than once per request. A network that lives there cannot be a model behind an API. It has to be a few hundred lines of arithmetic in the engine’s own language, run on integers, and updated incrementally as moves are made rather than recomputed from scratch, which is the whole trick of NNUE. The inference, in other words, had to be hand-written anyway. Once it was, the trainer was the same arithmetic run backwards, over a million parameters and inputs that are almost all zero, and it fitted in a few hundred lines too. Writing it is also how I found out what the framework would have hidden from me: the one constant I guessed instead of fitting turned a winning network into a losing one, and I would not have known why.

Rust is the language I write everything on this site in, from the neuron culture to the fantasy console, and it is the right tool for an engine for the usual reasons: no garbage collector in a loop that runs a million times a second, control over memory layout, and a compiler that produces WebAssembly with vector instructions from the same source as the native binary. One language runs from the self-play games on the laptop to the move on the phone, in one repository, and the web app has no build step. The trade-off is honest too. Training a small, sparse network on the CPU is fine. If the Go network ends up as a convolutional net with millions of dense parameters, Rust on ten cores will be slow, and I will have to decide whether to write a Metal kernel or admit that this is where the laptop study meets a GPU.

Why WebAssembly

Because the phone is the point. An opponent that lives on a server is not mine; an opponent in an app store is somebody else’s to approve. A web page that I add to my home screen, that works on a plane, and that runs the identical binary to the one on my laptop is the version I wanted, and in 2026 the browser can do it. WebAssembly has had 128-bit vector instructions for a while, and Safari now lets a page share memory between threads if it is served with the right isolation headers, so the chess engine on my phone searches on four cores. Lichess, the free chess site, runs Stockfish the same way for its analysis board, which was my proof that the approach was sound before I started.

The constraint also shaped the design more than any paper did. A network that has to be downloaded with the page and run on a phone has to be small; Kishi’s chess network is 820 kilobytes and is compiled into the engine binary. A search that has to run in a browser tab has to be frugal. Every decision that looks like taste in the code is really the phone saying no to something.

What happened

The chess engine came first: bitboards, a search with the usual family of pruning heuristics, and a hand-written evaluation borrowed from a well-known set of piece-square tables. Against Stockfish configured the way lichess configures its computer opponents, with twenty games a level on one core, it beats level 4 nineteen games to one, beats level 6 thirteen to seven, and loses to level 7 nineteen and a half to a half. If you have played the lichess computer, that places it: a solid club player, nowhere near the top.

Then the loop. The engine played itself from random openings for fifty-two minutes, which produced 5.6 million positions from fifty-seven thousand games, each labelled with what the search thought of it and how the game ended. A network trained on those positions in under twenty minutes beat the hand-written evaluation it replaced by 85 rating points, plus or minus 32, when both sides were allowed the same number of positions to look at. When both sides were allowed the same number of milliseconds, they came out even, because the network costs two and a half times as much per position. That is the whole problem of this kind of learning in one sentence, and I did not understand it before I had the numbers.

Shogi got its own engine with the same shape and a hand-written evaluation, which beats Fairy-Stockfish’s weakest setting twenty games to none and loses to a middling one eighteen to two. Go got the method of the late 2000s, Monte Carlo tree search with the shape patterns from the old MoGo program, and against GNU Go at its lowest level, with a second a move, it wins three games in ten. All three play on the phone. The chess one is the only one I would call a satisfying opponent at the top levels, and that is with the hand-written evaluation, because the trained network has not yet earned its place on the clock.

What this opened up

I started with one question, whether I could build Levy’s three parts, and I have ended the month with five better ones.

The chess network wins at equal search and draws at equal time. Does that change after more generations of self-play, as the games it learns from get stronger, or is a laptop-sized network always going to be paying for its own cost? The loop is running as I write this, at low priority, so the laptop stays usable. Why did one constant swing the result by 176 rating points, and what does that say about the contract between a learned component and the hand-tuned system it plugs into? Does the same loop work for shogi once the network can see where the kings are, which is what Nasu’s original design did and mine does not yet? Go needs the second kind of loop, where the search teaches the network which moves to look at, and I do not know what a laptop can train on a full nineteen-by-nineteen board; the AlphaGo chapters of the book, which I am about to reach, will tell me what it took in 2016, and I want to know what it takes in 2026 on a machine from a shop. And underneath all of it: how much of an engine’s strength survives the trip from a native binary to a browser tab on a phone, and what threads buy back.

Each of those is a few days of work and a few numbers, and I have started keeping a notebook in the repository so that the numbers are written down as they arrive, failures included. If the answers turn out to be as interesting as the questions, this may become the first of several pieces, one idea at a time, chess first, then shogi, then Go. Let’s see.

References

  • Sebastian Mallaby, The Infinity Machine: Demis Hassabis, DeepMind, and the Quest for Superintelligence (Penguin Press, 2026), chapters 1 to 5.
  • Claude Shannon, Programming a Computer for Playing Chess, Philosophical Magazine (1950).
  • David Levy, The Chess Computer Handbook (Batsford, 1984).
  • Yu Nasu, Efficiently Updatable Neural-Network-based Evaluation Functions for Computer Shogi (2018, in Japanese); Stockfish, Introducing NNUE Evaluation (2020).
  • David Silver and others, Mastering the game of Go with deep neural networks and tree search, Nature (2016).
  • Kishi: the engines, the training loop, and the notebook of every run.

entry.title: A capability, democratised
entry.content:
Making software used to be reserved for people with a particular privilege: the money to pay a team, or the team itself, or the years it takes to learn to program well enough to build something real. The power I wrote about is that privilege, democratised. Anyone with an idea, a subscription, and the patience to describe what they want can now have it built, and the ones who learn to describe well get a great deal.

Democratised capabilities have a history, and the history has a shape. Nobody who built the printing press or the web could say what people would do with them, and what people did was not on anyone’s plan. The web’s version of that story is in The Web Was the Training Set: a protocol given away, and thirty years of uses nobody at CERN drew. It emerged, from millions of small decisions, and it was better for almost everyone, collectively and in the end, even where it was hard for the people in the middle of it. I expect the same of this, with the same caveat; the move to the city is the comparison I keep returning to. And I expect the window in which it is an advantage rather than a baseline to be short, for the reason in the window before the utility.

entry.title: The move to the city
entry.content:
The comparison I keep coming back to is the move from the land to the city. The industrial cities of the nineteenth century were dense, dirty and short of everything, sanitation first of all; people got sick in them and died in them. The people still on the land did not want to go, and thought life was better where they were, and for them, in their own lifetimes, it often was. Over generations the move made almost everyone better off, and nobody now argues for going back; the long series is on Our World in Data’s page on urbanisation, below.

The thinking today has the same shape. The fear of what AI does to work is legitimate on the timescale of a life, and the long-run reading, that a democratised capability ends up better for everyone collectively, is probably also right. Both can be true, and the part that history does not make comfortable is the middle: the tumult in between.

References

  • Our World in Data, Urbanization: the share of people living in cities over two centuries, by country.

entry.title: The Web Was the Training Set
entry.content:
I read This Is for Everyone on the shore in Okinawa in the autumn of 2025 and wrote about it that winter in Looking back on 2025. That piece was about reefs and the open web. This one is about a sentence I read past the first time and cannot get out of my head a year later, after twelve months of building agent platforms for a living. It is the last line of the last chapter: “AI had aced the Imitation Game, and the web provided the data that made it possible.”

Berners-Lee writes it as a coda. I think it is the thesis of the book, and I think he undersells it.

What the book is

Three books share the binding. The first is a memoir: a boy in East Sheen whose parents wrote code for the Ferranti Mark 1 and knew Alan Turing, physics at Oxford, a homebrew computer built from factory-reject transistors and an adding machine fished out of a skip at a timber yard, a first job at Plessey in Poole. The second is the history everyone buys the book for: CERN, the 1989 memo, the NeXT cube, the first server, Mosaic, the World Wide Web Consortium. The third is a manifesto for the next thirty years: data sovereignty, Solid pods, and an AI that works for you rather than for the company that trained it. Stephen Witt, who wrote The Thinking Machine about Nvidia, is the co-author, and the prose is clean. The structure is looser. The book proceeds by association, which suits its subject, and which is also why some reviewers found it shapeless.

Compressed into one argument: the web won because it was universal and free, both qualities are now being eroded from the inside, and the way out is to give people control of their own data so that the next layer, the agents, works for them. I think he would accept that summary.

The epicentre was not where you expect

The book is strongest as geography. The web did not come out of Silicon Valley, and Berners-Lee is careful to say he barely knew the place existed when he graduated. In 1977, he writes, no Silicon Valley recruiter came to Oxford. His computing education came from his parents, from Manchester by way of Ferranti, and from the strange luck of being born in 1955, the year after Turing died, into a house with the Mark 1’s punch tape on the floor.

Switzerland comes before CERN. His first job abroad was in Zug, writing microprocessor code for a wafer saw, and he dates his attachment to the country to a night of Kaffee Fertig in a chalet above the cows: “I think it was then that I first fell in love with Switzerland. I’m still in love with it today.” CERN follows, first as a six-month contract in 1980 and then as a fellowship from 1984, with an apartment in Saint-Genis across the French border and windsurfing on the lake. The web was conceived in that corridor, at the coffee counter where people from twenty countries worked out how to run a machine nobody fully understood. The 1989 memo says so in its first argument: “CERN is a model in miniature of the rest of the world in a few years’ time. CERN meets now some problems which the rest of the world will have to face soon.”

What I had forgotten is how precarious the whole thing was. The question that hung over the project, in his own phrasing, was “Why, exactly, is the European taxpayer financing the oddball passion project of a thirty-six-year-old computer programmer in the Data and Documents division of a Franco-Swiss particle physics laboratory?” The answer, for three years, was that two managers, Mike Sendall and Peggie Rimmer, chose to hide him from the budget. Sendall’s pencilled “vague, but exciting” on the memo is famous. The chapter around it, about Sendall’s illness and the marriage Peggie entered to be able to care for him in a Swiss hospital, is the most human thing in the book, and it is a reminder that infrastructure gets built because particular people protect it for a while.

The British bookend is the 2012 Olympics, where Danny Boyle asked him to type the title phrase on a NeXT in front of 80,000 people as one of the inventions “Britons had shared with the world.” Between Geneva and London there is the one scene I would put in every history of computing: the 1992 NeXT developer conference in Paris, where Berners-Lee set up the web on a folding table to show Steve Jobs, and an aide pulled Jobs away one table early. He calls it a sliding-doors moment. I think he is right, and I think the door that closed was a European one. Two years later the consortium went to MIT, with a foothold at INRIA. The centre of gravity followed the money.

Free, because Gopher was not

The chapter I would make mandatory reading for anyone who writes policy about open standards is the one about Gopher. Until 1994 more people used Gopher than the web. In February 1993 the University of Minnesota announced that it reserved the right to charge licensees. It never collected a cent, by his account, and the announcement alone killed the protocol within months.

Berners-Lee’s reaction is the part that matters. He realised the web was in the same position: written on CERN machines, on a CERN salary, owned by CERN. “For the web to succeed, it had to be free.” Inside the lab there was a faction, he calls them “patriots”, who wanted the opposite: spin the web out as a company “to prove that Europe could compete” with Silicon Valley. He was sympathetic and overruled them. On 30 April 1993 CERN’s directors signed a statement that “CERN relinquishes all intellectual property rights to this code, both source and binary and permission is given to anyone to use, duplicate, modify and distribute it.”

I agree with the decision and I want to be exact about what it cost. Europe funded the research, hosted the invention, and gave away the result without keeping an institution that could compound on it. The protocol stayed free; the platforms built on top of it did not, and none of the large ones are European. That pattern, the commons funded here and captured there, is the background to the argument I made in The Bottleneck Is Data, and Europe Is Sitting on It, and reading this chapter again made me more convinced of it, not less. The public-domain release was correct. The absence of any European plan for what came after was the mistake, and it was not his to make.

The web was the training set

Now the sentence. Berners-Lee’s own account of machine learning is short and, for a man who spent two decades on the semantic web, generous. Machine learning, he writes, “has three legs: software, hardware and data,” and “it is the third leg, the data, that is in many cases the missing piece of the puzzle.” He tells the GPT story with the detail I had not registered: the first GPT trained on a corpus of self-published romance and science fiction, and “its output was closer to nonsense than meaningful human prose.” The models became useful only once OpenAI turned to the non-profit archivists at Common Crawl and trained on the web itself. His conclusion, in the chapter on intelligent machines: “Data was the fuel for this breakthrough” and, specifically, free and open web data.

The numbers back him. In the GPT-3 paper, filtered Common Crawl is 410 billion tokens and 60 per cent of the training mix by weight; the rest is more web (WebText2), two book corpora, and Wikipedia, which is also the web. The 2024 PNAS study he cites as the Turing Test being passed found that a GPT-4 model’s choices in behavioural games were statistically indistinguishable from a random person drawn from tens of thousands of human subjects in more than fifty countries. Whatever one thinks of the framing, the mechanism is not in dispute. The models learned to write from what people had published, and people had published it because of the thing this book describes.

What I want to add is why the web worked as a corpus, because the reasons are design decisions in chapters 2 and 3, not accidents. A page is a document with a stable address. Text is marked up, so titles and headings and lists can be told apart. Links are explicit, so relevance can be computed; PageRank is a graph algorithm over anchor tags, and Common Crawl’s filters and deduplication lean on the same structure. The hash sign, the place where in his words networking and hypertext “meet”, is also where a crawler learns which part of an address is a document and which is a position inside it. He describes the five-star ladder for open government data later in the book: on the web, structured, non-proprietary, addressable, linked. The web as a whole climbed that ladder without being asked, and a quarter of a century of people exposing their writing to each other in a structured, addressable form is what a transformer was eventually pointed at. The commons was the dataset before anyone called it one.

Two consequences follow, and the book reaches the first but not the second.

The first is his. The same openness that let the web grow is why the text could be taken without asking. He is blunt that Common Crawl “contains a lot of copyrighted material” and that the models can reproduce it, and he lands on a position I did not expect from the man who refused to patent HTTP: “An AI should only have the right to use your creative work as input if you have explicitly opted in, and should you opt in, you have a right to get paid.” He proposes a Content ID for text and admits the attribution problem is unsolved, with a GPT-4 ode to a dishwasher in the style of Philip Larkin as the test case. Nothing in it is Larkin’s, and all of it is. This site, for what it is worth, publishes a Content-Signal line in its robots.txt and a llms.txt and asks for attribution, which is roughly his opt-in with the terms attached. Whether anyone reads it is a separate question.

The second is mine. If the web was the training set, then what was never put on the web is not in the models. That is the whole of the European data argument in one line. The archives, the press runs, the parliamentary records, the century of paywalled newspaper pages, the scientific proceedings in twenty-four languages, exist in machine-readable form or could, and sit outside the corpus the frontier models were built from. Berners-Lee’s own life makes the point: the data at CERN only became valuable to physics once his system put it where other people could find it, and the same is true of the data Europe is sitting on now. The next increment of model quality is not in a larger crawl of the same web. It is in the material the web never got.

Where I disagree with him is on the mechanism of intelligence. He argues that scale settles the question: feed a model “a high proportion of all the sentences in the whole world” and “it builds a network with the number of nodes comparable to the number of neurons in your brain.” Parameters are not neurons and the comparison is loose; I read it as enthusiasm, not as a claim he would defend at a whiteboard. He also makes the stronger philosophical claim that there is no difference between simulating consciousness and having it. He is entitled to that view, and I would have liked a chapter on it rather than a paragraph.

Engineering lore

The chapters on the first year of the web are the most fun for anyone who ships software, and they are honest about regret in a way founders rarely are. The URL, in his account, was “the most important thing I ever wrote”, a few lines of code that reduced the friction of moving between machines to a click. The rule for the whole design was to reuse what people already knew: SGML for the markup, DNS for the names, Apollo workstation paths for the addressing. The double slash came from Apollo, and he apologises for it. The DNS order came from the United States, and he wishes he had used the British convention, most general part first, so that addresses read uk.co.widgets.www. The read-write browser he built on the NeXT, where every page was editable, lost to read-only browsers because users preferred one tool for reading and another for writing, and the web became “a lot more passive” than he intended. Marc Andreessen added the IMG tag to Mosaic unilaterally while the argument about a more general design was still running, which is exactly what a public-domain standard permits. The whole first browser, editor and all, was 9,555 lines of Objective-C.

There is a sentence in there for people who build platforms: “software designers, like urban planners, make the mistake of demanding that the user acts like the system, rather than the other way around.” The system behind the web is rigidly modernist, he says; the web on top of it was designed to be an anarchic jumble. Most of the platforms I have seen fail did so by letting the first layer leak into the second.

Charlie, and who the agent works for

The last third of the book is about Solid, the protocol for personal data pods that Berners-Lee has been building since the semantic web years, and about Inrupt, the company he co-founded to commercialise it. The argument runs through a 2017 dialogue with an imagined assistant called Charlie. Charlie reads a chef’s cookbooks as a training set to reconstruct a dish, invests in a start-up to give Bob something in common with his mother-in-law, and when asked who it works for answers: “Legally, ethically and algorithmically, I work for you, Bob.” It was written before ChatGPT, and it reads now like a product spec for the agents everyone is building.

As someone who builds the other side of that spec, I think he has the problem right and the solution only half right. The problem is real: the apps on a phone do not share data because they do not trust each other and do not speak the same language, and the agent that gets access to everything is the one that most needs to be trustworthy. That is the point of a context layer, which I have argued is the product and a write path, not a cache. Pods are a reasonable place to put that layer. They say nothing about who runs the model that reads it, where the inference happens, or what the agent is allowed to do with what it reads, and that is where the agent platforms I work on spend most of their effort. A pod makes the data yours. It does not make the agent yours.

The Solid chapters also read like a pitch, which they are, and Publishers Weekly’s complaint that the scheme “sounds fuzzy and dull” in his telling is fair. The ideas are not dull. The telling is, because it is written from inside the company. I would have cut a third of it.

Verdict

I give it 8 out of 10. The history is first-rate and told by the one person who can tell it, with the Swiss and British years given their due and the Gopher chapter alone worth the price. The AI chapters contain the most important idea in the book, that the web is the reason the models exist, and then leave it to the reader to work out what follows. The Solid chapters are a prospectus. The structure wanders, and the forecast is thin next to the history; John Arlidge in The Times called it 400 pages with no driving narrative, which is harsh and not entirely wrong.

Read it if you build anything on the web or on models trained from it, and read it for the history first. You do not need a technical background; the hardest idea in the book is the hash sign, and he explains it in a paragraph. Pair it with Mallaby’s The Infinity Machine, which I am reading now and which picks up the Hassabis thread this book opens at a Google dinner in 2014. And read the last line again when you are done. He provided the data. The question of what we do with the rest of it is still open, and it is a European question more than he lets on.
